title: Children's rights
hookLine: a good name, education, fairness between them

lines: ONE QUESTION: THE SAME FOR EACH?
cards: The boy in this story is the one who told it. Nu'man ibn Bashir remembered his father walking him to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. His father had given him a gift and wanted the Prophet to witness it.
The Prophet asked one question: had he given the same to each of his children? No. And the Prophet would not witness it.
Nu'man remembered his father taking the gift back. Today: what children are owed in Islamic law, and why fairness sits at the center.

teach.b: Day two hundred seventy-one showed the Prophet's tenderness with children. Today is the law's side. The fiqh books talk about a child's rights the way they talk about a spouse's: things owed, not favors.
First, a good name. Reports in Sahih Muslim tell of the Prophet changing harsh or heavy names into gentler ones.
A name is said across a whole life, by teachers and friends and, one day, on a grave, so choosing it well counts among a parent's duties.

A report in Ibn Majah calls seeking knowledge a duty on every Muslim, and jurists teach that a parent owes a child the teaching that makes it possible: how to read, how to pray, how to live with people, and a way to earn a living.
Third, fairness, and here is Nu'man's story again.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet tells his father to fear God and be just between his children. Not identical in every detail, since children need different things, but no child made to feel like the favorite's shadow.
The jurists argue over the edges: some hold that gifts to sons and daughters should be exactly equal; others follow the shares of inheritance.
Both start from the same story, where favoritism is a wrong, not a private taste.
And underneath all three, the Qur'an forbids killing children out of fear of poverty, and promises that God provides for them and for their parents. Before a name or a lesson comes life itself.

how: Islamic law counts choosing a good name and teaching a child to read, pray and earn a living among a parent's duties; scholars teach that gifts between children should be fair, following the story of Nu'man ibn Bashir.

o: what a child is owed: life, a good name, an education, fairness
favors parents give the child they feel closest to
freedoms a child earns on coming of age under the law

p: the boy whose gift went back
a duty a parent helps fulfill
fear God and be just between them

s: the Prophet agreed to witness a gift a father gave to only one son
he asked if every child had the same, and when the father said no, he would not witness it.
the story of the gift is told by the son who received it
Nu'man ibn Bashir, the boy, is the one who reports it.
the jurists agree on exactly how gifts between sons and daughters should be divided
some say exactly equal, others follow inheritance shares; the story itself treats favoritism as a wrong.

games.q: you're Bashir. you've given one son a gift and walked him to the Prophet to witness it. he asks if all your children got the same. they didn't. what happens?
o: the Prophet tells you to fear God and be just, and you take the gift back.
the Prophet tells you to give it to the eldest instead.
games.why: the Prophet would not witness it, told him to be just between his children, and the father took the gift back.

practice: Bring to mind the children in your life: your own, nieces and nephews, students, the kids on your street. Picture them in a row.
Notice if one face comes easier than the others, the funny one, the one who looks like you; no guilt, just notice.
Then go down the row slowly and give each one a moment of real attention, their name and one thing they need that is theirs alone, and if you pray, hold each name in turn.

wordCard.voice: Children's rights. In Islamic law, what a child is owed: life, a good name, an education, and fairness between them and their brothers and sisters. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: fair to each. No child left in the favorite's shadow. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2587; Sahih Muslim 1623 (Nu'man ibn Bashir's gift)
Sunan Ibn Majah 224 (seeking knowledge a duty)
